answer.text: Both long call and long put option positions
Both short call and short put positions

explanation.text: The Logic: Gamma measures the rate of change of delta with respect to the underlying price — geometrically, the curvature of the option's value curve. Because the value curves of both long call and long put are convex in the underlying, their delta increases as the underlying rises, so gamma is positive for any long option position (call or put). Selling those options inverts the convexity, making gamma negative for short calls and short puts. The sign of gamma therefore depends on long-vs-short, not call-vs-put. The Trap: "Only long calls" and "only short calls" wrongly tie gamma's sign to call/put. "Both short call and short put" gets the direction backwards — short options always carry negative gamma. The clean rule is: long options = positive gamma, short options = negative gamma. Note: The cited NISM Series VIII Equity Derivatives workbook defines gamma as the change in delta per unit change in the underlying and gives a call-gamma example, but the pages checked do not explicitly state the gamma-sign rule for long vs short calls and puts. The convexity reasoning above is general options-theory knowledge.
